title: Women In Garbage

jokes.text: How old is that handkerchief? / Well, it's not a handkerchief. It's a receipt.
jokes.setup: Leslie appears to notice a very old, worn piece of paper and assumes it's a handkerchief given Paula's age
jokes.punchline: Paula clarifies it's a receipt, implying it's so aged and worn it looks like a cloth — a visual gag about the ancient receipt and Paula's age
jokes.explanation: Quick, clean visual gag with good economy. The misdirection — assuming decrepit paper is a handkerchief — is funny and efficiently landed. Not deeply character-specific but works as an opener.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is beautiful. What is this fabric? Is it linen?

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: That's a Target receipt from 1987.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You've been carrying this around for... how long?

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: I don't know. A while.

jokes.text: They smoked their cigars, they snapped my bra, wore mirrors on their shoes to look up my skirt.
jokes.setup: Paula is recounting what it was like in government in the '70s boys' club
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from generic bad behavior (cigars) to specific, absurdly pervy harassment (mirror shoes) — played casually as fond memory
jokes.explanation: Strong escalating list joke — starts mundane (cigars), gets worse (bra-snapping), peaks with the specific absurdity of mirror shoes. The deadpan casualness of a senior citizen listing this as normal adds a dark subversive layer. Well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Women have come so far in Pawnee. We've broken through glass ceilings, shattered barriers, and now we hold positions of real power and influence.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But there's still one thing we can't do: approve a pothole repair without getting signed off on by three male department heads, a notary public, and the ghost of the town's founder.

jokes.text: Well, I am happy to report that it is now a pervert-free people's club. Well, except for Councilman Dexhart, who's a self-described pervert.
jokes.setup: Leslie pivots from Paula's horrifying story to say things have improved
jokes.punchline: She immediately qualifies her optimistic claim with the Dexhart caveat — a recurring character joke that undercuts her cheerfulness
jokes.explanation: The immediate self-correction is structurally tight. 'Self-described pervert' is a great specific detail — it implies Dexhart has publicly identified this way, which is funnier than just being accused of it. Very Parks-specific world-building humor.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: So first there was the cigar smoking in the office, which is fine, whatever. Then he started making comments about my appearance. Then he cornered me in the supply closet and tried to kiss me. Then he showed me his—

jokes.text: All the other councilmen used to keep a calendar of my menstrual cycle. / Are you kidding me? That is horrible. They don't do that to me. Do they do that to me?
jokes.setup: Paula reveals the men kept a menstrual calendar as a way to dismiss her; Leslie reacts with horror
jokes.punchline: Leslie's horror immediately pivots to paranoid self-interest — 'Do they do that to me?' — revealing her insecurity beneath her feminist outrage
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. The pivot from righteous indignation to 'Do they do that to ME?' is perfectly Leslie — simultaneously feminist champion and anxious self-monitor. The structure is clean: outrage, solidarity, then surprising self-focus. Very character-specific; no other character could land this beat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The government is now pervert-free!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Except for Jerry. He's still here.

jokes.text: I once tried to start a commission to get more jobs for women in city government, and they dismissed me, saying it was just my time of the month. Admittedly, they were right. Because of the calendar.
jokes.setup: Paula describes being dismissed with a sexist excuse
jokes.punchline: She concedes their dismissal was accurate — but only because they had literally been tracking her cycle with a calendar. The dark twist reframes the sexism as a circular, self-fulfilling prophecy.
jokes.explanation: This is the standout joke of the cold open. It's a genuine misdirection — we expect her to push back on the sexist dismissal, but she concedes — followed by a callback that recontextualizes the earlier joke. The logic is airtight and darkly funny: the sexist tool they used to dismiss her is the very thing that made their dismissal correct. High originality, beautifully structured.

jokes.text: You know what, I think men are better than women. She's kidding. / No, I'm not. They provide for us, and we must obey them because they are our masters.
jokes.setup: Leslie is fired up about starting a women's equality commission; April undercuts the moment
jokes.punchline: April delivers maximum anti-feminist provocation with complete deadpan sincerity, specifically designed to irritate Leslie
jokes.explanation: Classic April chaos-agent move — undermining Leslie's earnest cause with perfect deadpan. 'They are our masters' escalates nicely. Somewhat predictable for April's character archetype but well-executed. The double beat (Leslie's correction, April's rejection of the correction) tightens it.

dialogue.speaker: Paula Peverley
dialogue.line: They said I was being dismissed for hormonal reasons during my period.

dialogue.speaker: Paula Peverley
dialogue.line: But they were technically correct. I do keep a calendar.

jokes.text: April, stop it. / Leslie, you'll never land a beau with that domineering tone.
jokes.setup: Leslie scolds April for her anti-feminist trolling
jokes.punchline: April extends the bit by adopting the register of a 1950s etiquette guide, chiding Leslie for being too dominant
jokes.explanation: 'Land a beau' is a great period-specific word choice that makes April's troll more specific and funnier. The callback escalation adds value. April staying in character through Leslie's scolding is the comedic commitment that sells it.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I don't believe in gender equality. I think women are already superior and I'm tired of people pretending it's still a debate.

jokes.text: We must always walk behind the men. [Sheugh sound]
jokes.setup: April has been trolling Leslie with exaggerated anti-feminist statements; Leslie tries to move on
jokes.punchline: April extends the bit into a physical walking-behind gesture with a dismissive grunt, implying she's now literally acting it out as they leave the room
jokes.explanation: The tag on the running joke — April physically enacting her bit as they walk out. The 'Sheugh' sound is a dismissive noise, implying she's gesturing with grandiose deference. Earns rewatch value for the physicality, though the bit has run its course by this point.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Your beau needs to work on his tone. He sounds like he's constantly angry at a sandwich.

jokes.text: Moustache! Dumb-dumb!
jokes.setup: Ron is babysitting Diane's young daughters; we cut to him playing with them
jokes.punchline: Ron — a stoic, dignified man — is enthusiastically playing some kind of children's game involving yelling 'Moustache! Dumb-dumb!' with complete commitment
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character integration. The comedy is entirely dependent on WHO is saying this. Ron Swanson's stoic, hyper-masculine persona being fully committed to screaming nonsense children's game phrases is peak Parks & Rec. The absurdity is maximized through minimum words — 'Moustache! Dumb-dumb!' needs no explanation. Instant reaction laugh.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Women shouldn't be allowed to vote or own property. We're too emotional and our brains are smaller.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: *disgusted grunt*

jokes.text: Girls, this is Ann. Talk to Ann. She's terrific.
jokes.setup: Ann arrives and Ron is watching two young girls
jokes.punchline: Ron immediately and seamlessly tries to hand off the children to Ann with a salesman's pitch ('She's terrific'), suggesting he's desperate for relief
jokes.explanation: 'She's terrific' as a selling point to get children to like Ann — delivered in Ron's characteristically efficient manner — is funny. The speed of his pivot (no preamble, just 'Talk to Ann') suggests he's been waiting for an exit. Good economy.

dialogue.line: Innocent kid insults delivered with enthusiasm

jokes.text: Hey, dudettes. You stoked about the weekend? / No. / Oh, look at this pwetty, pwetty wittle beads. / They're not infants. / I don't know. I'm weird with kids. / So you guys like Coldplay?
jokes.setup: Ann tries to connect with Diane's young daughters and fails spectacularly at multiple attempted registers
jokes.punchline: Each attempt is worse than the last — teen-speak, baby talk (immediately corrected), self-aware confession, then the desperately uncool Coldplay offer
jokes.explanation: Classic cringe escalation — each correction makes Ann's next attempt worse. 'They're not infants' from Ron is a perfectly deadpan parenting correction. 'So you guys like Coldplay?' is the perfect embarrassing final attempt — specifically Coldplay, not a generic band, makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm entertaining the kids by letting them play with toys I borrowed from you people at work.

jokes.text: You're weird. / You're... / Well, hey, girls. / No.
jokes.setup: Ron attempts his own greeting after Ann's failed attempts
jokes.punchline: The child immediately rejects Ron with 'No' — his greeting gets the same treatment as Ann's, undercutting the idea that Ron would do any better
jokes.explanation: The child's flat 'No' as a complete sentence is a small but clean joke — the kid rejecting adults' attempts at connection. Ron's unfinished 'You're...' suggests he was about to return the insult before stopping himself, which adds a layer.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Hey kids, what's up? That's tight! That's da bomb! We can kick it, fo shizzle!

jokes.text: Leslie, I don't think this is a good idea. / I think it's a fantastic idea. / Oh. / I didn't know where you were going with that.
jokes.setup: Chris expresses doubt; Leslie declares confidence; Chris reacts
jokes.punchline: Chris's 'Oh. I didn't know where you were going with that' — delivered as if it was a genuine surprise that Leslie disagreed — is both a character joke (Chris's relentless positivity) and a structural punchline
jokes.explanation: Good Chris Traeger character joke — his confusion that someone would disagree with him, delivered as innocent bewilderment. The economy is tight: the joke is entirely in the pause ('Oh.') and self-reflection. Very character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Hey there, little guy! Ooh, who's a precious baby? You are! Yes, you are!

dialogue.speaker: Kid
dialogue.line: I'm nine.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh... well, who's a precious nine-year-old? You are!

jokes.text: She's my special friend. / That's what you're calling her now. / I don't know what to call her. / I don't entirely understand the behavior of young people. Recently, we engaged in something called a 'group hang.' It was like a date, but there were seven other people there. It was very confusing.
jokes.setup: Chris refers to Shauna Malwae-Tweep as his 'special friend,' and Leslie calls him out
jokes.punchline: Chris's confessional reveals he doesn't understand modern dating — specifically that he doesn't understand 'group hangs' as a concept — which is both observationally funny about contemporary ambiguous dating and absurdly funny given he's a middle-aged city manager
jokes.explanation: Chris's status anxiety about relationship labels is a strong character beat. 'Group hang' as a confused observation and the overly formal 'we engaged in something called' framing is funny. Good observational hook with character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Ann, you know that babies can't understand words, right? They just respond to tone and inflection. So talking to them like they're adults is actually more effective.

jokes.text: Labels can be bad, but they can also be good. 'Warning: Toxic bleach' is a good label.
jokes.setup: Chris rationalizes the question of labels in his relationship
jokes.punchline: His example of a 'good label' is 'Warning: Toxic bleach' — a completely off-topic, literal, and absurdly practical example that reveals he has entirely lost the thread of the romantic conversation
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The pivot from romantic relationship labels to consumer product safety warnings is unexpected, perfectly Chris — his relentless literal-mindedness applied to an emotional context — and the specific example ('Toxic bleach') is pitch-perfect. High quotability, high originality. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor: sharp, unexpected, highly quotable, great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: So, uh, do you guys like The Strokes?

jokes.text: Shauna Malwae-Tweep has amazing dimples.
jokes.setup: Chris wraps up the confessional with a practical note
jokes.punchline: After all the label anxiety and bleach tangent, Chris signs off by stating a simple fact about his attraction — 'amazing dimples' — as if this is a relevant piece of information
jokes.explanation: A small but effective button on the confessional — Chris's final line is a non-sequitur that reveals what he's actually thinking about. The abruptness is the joke. Works as an exit joke.

dialogue.speaker: Kid
dialogue.line: You're weird.

jokes.text: Okay, I know this text you sent me was a lie and Michael Stipe is not actually here, correct? / Correct. That was a lie. / Yeah, no, I knew it was. I just couldn't live with myself if it had been true. / And that's why I sent it.
jokes.setup: Tom texted Ben a false claim that Michael Stipe was at the office to get him to come
jokes.punchline: Ben admits he knew it was a lie but came anyway because he couldn't live with the possibility of it being true — and Tom confirms this is exactly why he used that lie
jokes.explanation: Strong character comedy — Ben's admission that he came anyway 'just in case' is a perfect nerd/fanboy character beat (Michael Stipe of R.E.M.), and Tom's confirmation that he calculated this exactly shows Tom's con-man cunning. The mutual awareness of the manipulation is what elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Wait, so a 'group hang' is when multiple people just... hang out together? Without any formal structure or predetermined outcome?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: That's fascinating. It's like observing a previously undocumented social ritual. Do they have a leader? A hierarchy? What are the resource allocation protocols?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: This changes everything I thought I knew about modern courtship.

jokes.text: Where's free Skittles? / Here you go, buddy. / Aw! / He gets his thing?
jokes.setup: Tom has also lured Andy with free Skittles
jokes.punchline: Ben's exasperated 'He gets his thing?' — implying Andy's bribe was as simple as candy while Ben required an R.E.M. celebrity sighting
jokes.explanation: Good character contrast joke — Andy's simplicity (Skittles suffice) vs. Ben's complexity (needs an R.E.M. legend). Ben's wounded reaction is the punchline. Efficient and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: You know, I think relationship labels are like hazardous material warnings. They're just there to protect people from something dangerous.

jokes.text: I can't keep referring to basketball players as 'Khloe Kardashian's husband and his friends.'
jokes.setup: Tom explains his basketball knowledge deficit to Andy and Ben
jokes.punchline: His actual working description of Lamar Odom (Khloe's then-husband) as a stand-in for not knowing any players by name is both a celebrity-culture punchline and a revealing character moment
jokes.explanation: Excellent Tom Haverford joke. That his only reference frame for NBA players is through Kardashian matrimony is perfectly character-specific — Tom lives in celebrity/pop-culture space rather than sports space. 'Khloe Kardashian's husband and his friends' as a team descriptor is genuinely funny and quotable. Strong originality.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: You know, Shauna, I have to say... those are some really nice shoulders you have. Very well-defined. And your bone structure is just... exceptional.

jokes.text: One jock, one geek who loves stats. I'll give you a few minutes to cancel the rest of your plans for the day. / No need. My only plan was to buy Skittles.
jokes.setup: Tom flatters Andy and Ben as the perfect basketball tutors and gives them a moment to clear their schedules
jokes.punchline: Andy's entire day plan was to buy Skittles — which he has already received — making Tom's flattery hilarious in hindsight
jokes.explanation: Good callback — Andy's Skittles plan pays off with perfect Andy-level life ambition. The contrast between Tom's 'cancel the rest of your plans' setup (implying a busy day) and Andy's nothing-day is character-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, where's Michael Stipe? I thought he was supposed to be here today!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, about that... nobody actually said Michael Stipe was coming.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What? But I've been preparing all morning! I learned all the lyrics to 'It's the End of the World as We Know It'!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy, we lied to you so you'd actually show up on time for work.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You guys are the worst.

jokes.text: Wow, Chris. Your gender equality commission is a real sausage fest.
jokes.setup: Leslie's new gender equality commission meeting room is being shown
jokes.punchline: Ben deadpans that the all-male commission is a 'sausage fest' — using a crass idiom in the context of a formal equality initiative
jokes.explanation: The irony of an all-male gender equality commission is strong situational comedy. 'Sausage fest' as Ben's word choice is slightly incongruous with his earnest character, which adds a mild surprise. Not deeply crafted but the situational irony does the work.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I knew that Michael Stipe thing was a total lie.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But I still had to Google it just to be sure.

jokes.text: Oh, there's a lady right next to you. / Oh, wait, no. / It's just a very beautiful man.
jokes.setup: Leslie notices there are no women and asks if anyone noticed
jokes.punchline: A man nearly identifies a woman in the room — then corrects himself that it's 'a very beautiful man' — a joke about gender presentation that also subtly mocks the commission's cluelessness
jokes.explanation: A quick visual/verbal gag that adds texture to the commission scene. 'Very beautiful man' is an odd enough phrase to get a chuckle. Functional but not deeply crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, so I need to learn about basketball. I've been studying the greats. You know, like that tall guy who plays for the Lakers? The one who's really good at dunking? I think his name is... Basketball Dunk Man?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And then there's the guy on the Celtics. Super talented. I call him... Green Shirt Bounce Guy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh! And the Miami Heat player? The one everyone talks about? I'm pretty sure his name is Swish Swish Points Man.

jokes.text: Listen, you did a great job setting it up and getting the snacks ready, but we'll take it from here.
jokes.setup: Leslie runs the gender equality commission; Councilman Milton patronizingly dismisses her contribution
jokes.punchline: Milton reduces Leslie's entire effort to 'snacks,' perfectly embodying the sexism the commission was created to fight — making the irony pointed and uncomfortable
jokes.explanation: Strong satirical joke — the sexist dismissal at a gender equality meeting is self-aware dramatic irony. The specific detail of reducing Leslie's work to 'snacks' is pointed and character-specific for Milton. The audience should feel both amused and outraged, which is exactly the intended effect.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hey, can you guys cancel your plans tonight? I need to talk to you about something important.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I can't. I have a very strict schedule. At 6 PM, I'm going to eat a plain chicken breast with steamed vegetables. At 7 PM, I'm going to do some light stretching. At 8 PM, I'm going to review my financial spreadsheets. And at 9 PM, I'm going to be asleep.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's your entire night?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: That's every night. It's called discipline, Tom. It's called living a life of purpose and meaning.

jokes.text: Round of applause for the girl. She has to leave to get more snacks.
jokes.setup: Leslie asserts herself at the commission; Milton doubles down
jokes.punchline: Milton escalates the condescension by rallying the room to applaud Leslie as she supposedly leaves for snacks — compounding the dismissal and making it a group act
jokes.explanation: Strong escalation of the previous joke — Milton mobilizes the room's applause, turning individual sexism into collective sexism. 'For the girl' is perfectly condescending. The joke works as both satire and cringe comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: It's entirely men

jokes.text: Ouch. Why so ornery? / It's not the 7th yet.
jokes.setup: Milton asks why Leslie is upset; an unnamed voice answers
jokes.punchline: 'It's not the 7th yet' — a callback to the menstrual calendar joke from earlier, implying someone in the room actually does track Leslie's cycle. The casual delivery makes it more horrifying and funnier.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional callback — the cold open's dark joke about Paula's colleagues keeping a menstrual calendar is now revealed to be still ongoing with Leslie. The five words 'It's not the 7th yet' are perfectly economical, horrifying, and hilarious simultaneously. The matter-of-fact delivery implies this is common knowledge in the room. The structural callback to Paula's story adds a thematic punch. This is the episode's best single line.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: You know, I've been looking at this council, and I have to say, there's a real lack of women represented here.

dialogue.speaker: Councilman Milton
dialogue.line: What are you talking about? There's a woman right there.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Where?

dialogue.speaker: Councilman Milton
dialogue.line: That beautiful blonde woman in the suit.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: That's Ben Wyatt. He's a man.

dialogue.speaker: Councilman Milton
dialogue.line: Well, he should be a woman. He's gorgeous.

jokes.text: Ron's reaction to the girls yelling 'Mommy!' and Diane arriving — 'Your shoes are red now. / Yay. / Hooray.'
jokes.setup: The girls are excited Diane is here; Ron is relieved
jokes.punchline: The girls celebrate Diane's arrival while Ron observes a non-sequitur ('Your shoes are red now') as if this is important information — suggesting the day has been chaotic enough that this detail stands out
jokes.explanation: Small visual gag — the girls have apparently gotten paint or something on Diane's shoes. 'Your shoes are red now' as Ron's deadpan observation is a gentle absurdist moment. Low stakes but adds texture to the babysitting chaos storyline.

dialogue.speaker: Councilman Milton
dialogue.line: Women are perfectly capable in government roles.

dialogue.speaker: Councilman Milton
dialogue.line: Leslie, be a dear and fetch us some snacks.

jokes.text: My sitter's still out of town, so I really hate to ask you this, but is there any way you could take them again tomorrow? / Of course. I'd be delighted.
jokes.setup: Diane apologetically asks Ron to watch the girls again after what was clearly a difficult day
jokes.punchline: Ron, who was clearly stressed, immediately and enthusiastically agrees — 'I'd be delighted' — revealing his genuine affection for Diane overrides all evidence of the day's difficulty
jokes.explanation: Good character joke — Ron's immediate 'I'd be delighted' after clearly suffering through the day is a warm comedic beat that reveals his feelings for Diane without stating them. Character-specific warmth.

dialogue.speaker: Councilman Milton
dialogue.line: Is it that time of the month?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Excuse me?

dialogue.speaker: Councilman Milton
dialogue.line: I'm just checking the calendar. You seem ornery.

jokes.text: I believe one problem with hiring women is that they're frail and breakable. / Is it possible you're thinking about light bulbs? / Or your hip?
jokes.setup: A councilman states his objection to hiring women in sanitation
jokes.punchline: Leslie's comeback — 'Is it possible you're thinking about light bulbs?' — is a controlled burn, and the addition of 'Or your hip?' from another voice extends it with a jab at Milton's age
jokes.explanation: 'Is it possible you're thinking about light bulbs?' is a razor-sharp comeback — matching the original's condescension with polite dismissal of his intellect. The 'Or your hip?' tag is a well-timed secondary punchline. Both lines would work in isolation; together they're stronger.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Why are you children writing on each other?

dialogue.speaker: Child
dialogue.line: We're not writing on each other. We're coloring his shoes.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: His shoes are already a color.

jokes.text: If I were 300 years older, Councilman.
jokes.setup: Milton apparently makes a flirtatious or inappropriate comment (implied from Leslie's response)
jokes.punchline: Leslie's comeback — 'If I were 300 years older, Councilman' — implies Milton is so ancient that only someone equally ancient would be appropriate for him, delivered as a withering brush-off
jokes.explanation: 'If I were 300 years older' is an excellent comeback — funny, specific in its exaggeration (not 30, not 100, but 300), and perfectly Leslie in its precise but biting tone. The 'Councilman' tag adds formal politeness that makes the insult more cutting. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Diane
dialogue.line: Ron, can you watch the kids again this weekend?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Of course, Diane. I would be delighted to spend time with your children. I have prepared a comprehensive schedule of activities involving woodworking, proper etiquette, and early bedtimes.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Everything will be perfectly orderly and under control.

dialogue.speaker: Child
dialogue.line: Dad, the kitchen's on fire!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That is merely a controlled learning experience about the dangers of negligence.

jokes.text: You have one woman, and she's a secretary. / And she's the best secretary we got, except for Dan. / Dan's awesome. / Dan.
jokes.setup: Leslie calls out the lack of female employees in Sanitation
jokes.punchline: The sanitation workers' defense — the one woman is great, BUT Dan (clearly a man) is better — and then two people spontaneously celebrating Dan, is absurdist and character-revealing
jokes.explanation: The spontaneous Dan appreciation — with multiple workers echoing 'Dan' — is a great Parks crowd joke. These men are unaware they're proving Leslie's point. The structure (Leslie's accusation → defense → inadvertent self-indictment) is clean. 'Dan.' as a reverent stand-alone utterance is the comedic button.

dialogue.speaker: Councilman
dialogue.line: Women are like fine china - beautiful to look at, but you can't use them for anything practical.

jokes.text: April, I love you, but I don't need your sarcasm right now. / I'm serious. Let's get rolling. / I wanna get into some garbage. / What? / I love garbage. / You ever found a dead body in the trash? Or body parts? Like, a torso or a head? / Please say head.
jokes.setup: Leslie is rallying April to prove themselves in sanitation; April is unexpectedly enthusiastic
jokes.punchline: April's genuine excitement about garbage reveals itself as specifically about dead body parts — culminating in 'Please say head,' which is both darkly funny and character-perfect
jokes.explanation: Exceptional April character comedy. The subversion of Leslie assuming April is being sarcastic (when she's genuinely enthusiastic) is good structure. But 'You ever found a dead body... please say head' is perfectly April — her macabre curiosity presented as completely casual. Very character-specific; no other character on the show could deliver this.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We have an excellent track record with female employees. Our best female employee is amazing.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Yes, but she's still behind Kevin in the rankings.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Kevin is a male secretary.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Exactly.

jokes.text: Hey, Dewey. Leslie brought binders. / What do they say? / 'Pick up garbage. Put in truck'? / Actually, yeah. That's what's in the binder on every page because I believe in being thorough.
jokes.setup: The sanitation workers mock Leslie's binder; Leslie defends it
jokes.punchline: The binder actually does just say 'Pick up garbage. Put in truck' on every page — confirming the mockery, but Leslie frames it as a virtue ('I believe in being thorough')
jokes.explanation: Great Leslie joke — her binder obsession turned against her, then turned into a virtue by Leslie herself. The structure is a double-subversion: we expect her to push back on Steve's mockery, but she confirms it, then reframes it. 'I believe in being thorough' as self-justification for an absurd binder is perfect Leslie character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know, I just want to say that garbage collectors are some of the most important people in our society. They're hardworking, they're dedicated, they're... smelly glue that holds our community together.

jokes.text: I thought your last name was Hanson for some reason. / No, it's Perkins. Always has been. / You seem more like a Hanson.
jokes.setup: Ron arrives at Ann's door having looked her up in the directory
jokes.punchline: Ron insists she 'seems more like a Hanson' — an absurdist non-judgment about someone's name-face fit that Ron delivers with complete seriousness
jokes.explanation: 'You seem more like a Hanson' is a beautifully absurd non-sequitur from Ron — a man who would never normally comment on anything so trivial. The joke is that Ron, of all people, has formed a strong opinion about her name-face fit. Great economy and character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I want to work in garbage. Not because I care about the environment or whatever, but because I want to find corpses.

jokes.text: Let's play a word association game. I'll say a word, and then you say the first thing that pops into your mind. / Okay. / You. / Reporter. / Me. / City manager. / Us. / Ooh! Magazine.
jokes.setup: Chris tries to define their relationship through a word association game
jokes.punchline: When he says 'Us,' hoping for a romantic response, Shauna says 'Magazine' — interpreting the word entirely literally, completely deflating Chris's romantic attempt
jokes.explanation: Very well-structured joke. The word association game is clever because it creates a pattern (You→Reporter, Me→City Manager) that makes 'Us' feel like it's building to something romantic. 'Magazine' is the perfect deflation — completely literal, not at all unkind, just oblivious. The structure builds and subverts cleanly. The 'Ooh!' before Magazine suggests Shauna is pleased to think of the magazine, making Chris's disappointment more poignant and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I've prepared detailed binders on every topic we could possibly discuss.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: Leslie, what's in these binders?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Everything. Comprehensive breakdowns, color-coded sections, backup materials...

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm just going to guess they contain pictures of parks.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: How did you—

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: I know you, Leslie.

jokes.text: According to Leslie's binder, she and April are making even better time than the guys do on a normal day. / Wow, that's weird. You know, with us being women and all, you'd think our boobs would get in the way. / Is that accurate, Mr. Phlegner? Is Councilwoman Knope ahead of the regular schedule for this route? / Whatever. No comment.
jokes.setup: Leslie and April are doing better than expected; Leslie mocks the sexist assumption
jokes.punchline: Leslie sarcastically echoes the sexist logic ('you'd think our boobs would get in the way') and then the sanitation worker's sour 'No comment' confirms he's annoyed because they're right
jokes.explanation: Leslie weaponizing the sexist assumption against the sexists is good comic construction. 'No comment' from Phlegner is the perfect sour reaction. The 'Is that accurate, Mr. Phlegner?' formal address to a garbage truck driver while triumphant is very Leslie.

jokes.text: Are you posing? / I don't have a photographer with me. / Google Earth... Always taking pics.
jokes.setup: April catches Leslie in some kind of triumphant pose on the garbage truck route
jokes.punchline: Leslie's excuse — Google Earth is always photographing — is a paranoid-but-charming Leslie justification for her vanity
jokes.explanation: 'Google Earth... always taking pics' as Leslie's reasoning for posing on a garbage route is a specific, funny character beat — her ego and optimism expressed in paranoid satellite-photograph self-awareness.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: You know, we've done soccer, we've done ballet, we've done chess club... I'm running out of activities for the kids.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I mean, at this point I'm like, 'What's next, we could just set up a land mine in the backyard?'

jokes.text: Eh, he's too big. I can't see over him. It's not fair. / I feel like everyone should be the same size.
jokes.setup: Andy is supposed to guard Tom during basketball practice but complains about a larger player
jokes.punchline: Tom's solution — 'I feel like everyone should be the same size' — is an absurdist non-answer that reveals Tom hasn't understood anything about basketball (or competitive life)
jokes.explanation: 'I feel like everyone should be the same size' is a perfectly useless response to a sports problem. It's Tom at his most helpless — applying aesthetic/social logic to a physical challenge. Good character specificity and nice economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wow, so we're doing better at this job than you guys. I guess that means we're better at everything. We should run the country. We should run the world.

dialogue.speaker: Male Garbage Worker
dialogue.line: That's not what this means.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, no, no. You started this. You implied that physical strength determines someone's worth as a person and as a professional. So clearly, since April and I are kicking your ass, we are now your superiors in every conceivable way.

jokes.text: Tommy for the dunk!
jokes.setup: Tom has been learning basketball and attempts a dunk
jokes.punchline: Tom narrates his own dunk attempt in the third person — implying it goes spectacularly wrong (visual context from the extended pause and the 'My screen!' line after)
jokes.explanation: Tom narrating his own dunk is character-specific (his self-delusion and showmanship). The physical comedy is inferred from the cut to chaos. The rewatch bonus is for seeing what presumably happens during the dunk attempt.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? No! I'm not posing. Why would I be posing? Do you know how many satellites are up there right now? Forty-seven. I counted. And they're all looking down. Always looking down. I can feel it on the back of my neck.

jokes.text: My screen!
jokes.setup: Tom's dunk attempt
jokes.punchline: Someone's phone/device has been destroyed in the basketball chaos — 'My screen!' implies a shattered phone, collateral damage from Tom's sports incompetence
jokes.explanation: A quick physical comedy beat — the specificity of a cracked phone screen is contemporary and relatable. Works better visually (rewatch bonus for the physical moment). Minimal craft in the writing itself; this is a production/acting joke.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I got it. I'm just gonna get really good at basketball really fast.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Like, I'm gonna watch some YouTube videos, do some drills, and by tomorrow I'll be unstoppable.

jokes.text: But it was actually a blood-hungry witch who was wearing their mom's face like a mask!
jokes.setup: Ann is telling the girls what she thinks is a fun ghost story
jokes.punchline: Ann's story turns grotesquely inappropriate — face-wearing witches — revealing her complete misread of what children's scary stories should be, right when Ron thought she had things under control
jokes.explanation: 'A blood-hungry witch wearing their mom's face like a mask' is specific enough to be genuinely disturbing — not generic horror but face-mask horror, which is several levels worse than a regular ghost story. The specificity makes it funnier. Ann's obliviousness to the inappropriateness is character-consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm playing basketball.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Tom, you're just standing there holding the ball.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, but am I though?

jokes.text: What is wrong with you, woman? / Sorry. I thought kids liked ghost stories.
jokes.setup: Ron reacts to Ann's blood-hungry witch story
jokes.punchline: Ann's defense — 'I thought kids liked ghost stories' — is a perfect, oblivious non-apology that completely misses why the specific story was wrong
jokes.explanation: The reaction beat works on Ron's genuine alarm and Ann's genuine defenselessness. 'I thought kids liked ghost stories' is obliviously accurate — kids DO like ghost stories, but not that ghost story. Good character contrast.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Did that go in?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I think that went in.

jokes.text: This is Stacy Knoblauch's house. I went to high school with her, and she was super mean to me, and now I know that she dyes her hair.
jokes.setup: Leslie and April are doing a garbage pickup at a private residence
jokes.punchline: Leslie pivots from feminist mission to petty high school score-settling — using her garbage route access to gather intel on a high school nemesis's hair color
jokes.explanation: Excellent Leslie character joke — her feminist mission immediately corrupted by petty personal grudges the moment opportunity arises. 'Now I know that she dyes her hair' as the vindictive payoff is perfect: the triumph is small, specific, and completely disproportionate to the gravitas Leslie assigns it.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Once upon a time, there were three little children who went into the woods...

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: And they never came back. Their bones were found scattered across the forest floor, picked clean by vultures.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: The end.

jokes.text: I knew that wench wasn't naturally blonde. / Oh, my God! / She has to use prescription-strength deodorant. / This is the best day of my life.
jokes.setup: Leslie has identified a high school enemy's garbage; April and Leslie discover her secrets
jokes.punchline: The escalating trash revelations — dye, then prescription deodorant — lead to Leslie's genuinely felt 'This is the best day of my life,' treating enemy-trash-intel as a profound feminist victory
jokes.explanation: The escalation from hair dye to prescription deodorant is a perfect comedic build — each revelation is more intimate and embarrassing than the last. April's 'I knew that wench wasn't naturally blonde' is her joining Leslie's petty energy with full commitment. 'This is the best day of my life' from Leslie — who is supposedly on a feminist mission — is the punchline that ties it all together. Very quotable, very character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I was just trying to teach them about the circle of life. I brought in a dead bird I found in my yard and showed it to all the kids. I thought it would be educational!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Ann.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What? It's natural! They need to understand that death is part of nature.

jokes.text: And some privacy to violate! / Yeah! / Whoo! / Wait, no.
jokes.setup: Leslie rallies April with 'We have some stereotypes to overcome!'
jokes.punchline: April adds 'And some privacy to violate!' — Leslie cheers this, then catches herself with 'Wait, no.'
jokes.explanation: The meta-acknowledgment that they just violated someone's privacy — and Leslie's delayed 'Wait, no' after enthusiastically cheering it — is a tight, well-structured callback. Leslie's self-correction too late is perfectly in character.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Hair dye. In the trash. Someone's covering something up.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm gonna find out who, and I'm gonna use it against them. Forever.

jokes.text: You are officially a baller. / I've been a baller since birth, son. / Now, I'm an athlete.
jokes.setup: Tom makes a basket and is validated
jokes.punchline: Tom's 'I've been a baller since birth, son' — said after barely learning to dribble — is a self-aggrandizing non-sequitur; 'Now, I'm an athlete' adds another layer of inflated self-assessment
jokes.explanation: Classic Tom grandiosity joke — immediately overclaiming achievement after a minor success. The distinction between 'baller' (pre-existing identity) and 'athlete' (newly earned) is a funny Tom-logic distinction. Character-specific but somewhat predictable Tom behavior.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, April, look at this! Ben threw away his high school yearbook with a note that says 'Too many memories of being unpopular.'

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's great. Can we go now?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, there's more! His old gym class photos where he's clearly struggling with the rope climb. This is gold, April. Pure gold.

jokes.text: This could really only go poorly.
jokes.setup: Tom challenges the actual kids to a basketball game after barely learning to play
jokes.punchline: Ben's deadpan talking-head assessment is an understatement that serves as perfect dramatic irony before what's clearly a disaster
jokes.explanation: Great economy — six words that perfectly summarize the situation. Ben as the voice of reason in a talking-head is a character-specific beat. The deadpan understatement ('could really only go poorly') is effective in its simplicity.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Oh my god. Oh my god, oh my god, oh my god. Ben threw away his grocery list and it says 'Activia.' Ben Wyatt drinks Activia.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: This is the best day of my life.

jokes.text: Tom, what the hell are you doing? / I'm pivoting. Ben told me to pivot. / I told you you can pivot, not that you can only pivot. Stop pivoting!
jokes.setup: Tom has apparently been pivoting continuously during the game
jokes.punchline: Tom has taken 'you can pivot' as a directive to pivot exclusively and constantly — a perfectly literal misapplication of advice that reveals his fundamental basketball ignorance
jokes.explanation: Excellent physical/verbal comedy. Tom pivoting endlessly is a great visual gag that lands through dialogue. Ben's frustrated correction — 'not that you can ONLY pivot' — is perfectly exasperated and clearly articulates why this is wrong without explaining the joke. 'Stop pivoting!' as a command you'd never expect to give someone is very funny. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm so excited about this project. I've been thinking about it all night.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's wonderful! What specifically has you so energized?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Well, I realized if we push this through, we can use the city funds to build that statue of our enemy in the town square so everyone has to look at his stupid face every day.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April... that's not— we can't just use public resources for personal vendettas.

jokes.text: You suck at basketball, man. / Well, you suck at being polite, sir.
jokes.setup: After the disastrous game, a kid calls Tom out
jokes.punchline: Tom's comeback — 'you suck at being polite, sir' — is a perfectly Tom response: refusing to accept the basketball criticism by pivoting to etiquette, and the formal 'sir' to a child is chef's kiss
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. Tom refuses to engage on the kid's terms (basketball) and redirects to a domain he can claim authority in (manners). 'Sir' addressed to a child is the key move — it's formal, it's slightly aggressive, and it reveals Tom's wounded dignity. Very character-specific and very quotable. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in sharpness and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: He's going to pull a hamstring and then sue the city.

jokes.text: Andy Dwyer for the dunk! / Aw, that wall's so close.
jokes.setup: Andy attempts his own dunk after the game
jokes.punchline: Andy narrates his own dunk (mirroring Tom's earlier failed attempt) then discovers the wall is too close — he presumably hits it, and his reaction 'Aw, that wall's so close' treats it as a mild inconvenience
jokes.explanation: The callback to Tom's failed dunk attempt with Andy's version is effective. 'Aw, that wall's so close' as Andy's response to walking into a wall is perfectly Andy — neither injured nor angry, just mildly surprised the wall is there. Rewatch bonus for the physical comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Tom, you can't just pivot whenever you want. That's traveling.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: But I'm pivoting!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yes, I can see that. That's the problem.

jokes.text: This is the most fun I have ever had with kids. They even said they wanted to be doctors when they grow up. Hot tip for you baby-sitters out there. Let your kids play with medical tools all the time.
jokes.setup: Ann's talking-head confessional about her success with the children and playing doctors
jokes.punchline: Ann gives parenting advice based on the immediately-about-to-go-wrong medical tools situation — the dramatic irony is maximum because we're about to see what 'medical tools' means for unsupervised children
jokes.explanation: The talking-head cuts RIGHT before or after discovering the chaos, making Ann's confident parenting advice ironically wrong in real-time. 'Hot tip for you baby-sitters out there' is a great faux-influencer voice that Ann uses unironically. Strong dramatic irony structure.

dialogue.speaker: Kid
dialogue.line: You're really bad at basketball.

jokes.text: Hot tip for you baby-sitters out there. Let your kids play with medical tools all the time.
jokes.setup: Ann is still in talking-head mode confidently endorsing giving children medical implements
jokes.punchline: She directly addresses the audience with ironically terrible parenting advice delivered as wisdom — the joke being that this is demonstrably about to go horribly wrong
jokes.explanation: Ann speaking directly to the camera with dangerous parenting advice in the tone of a lifestyle blogger is a great mockumentary joke. 'Hot tip for you baby-sitters out there' as an opener is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Child
dialogue.line: You're bad at basketball!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, I appreciate your passion for the sport. However, I would submit that my performance today was hampered by several external factors, including but not limited to: suboptimal court conditions, inadequate footwear, and the general chaos of this recreational facility. I'll have you know I was MVP of my church league in 2009.

jokes.text: We have a problem. / What? / Oh, my God. / Girls! This is not a negotiation. Unlock the door immediately. / No! / We're doing surgery! / Only doctors are allowed in here.
jokes.setup: The children have locked themselves in a room with Ann's medical kit and are doing 'surgery'
jokes.punchline: The girls refuse to unlock the door because 'only doctors are allowed' — they've fully committed to the surgery bit in a way that is now genuinely concerning
jokes.explanation: 'Only doctors are allowed in here' from a child who has locked adults out of a room with scissors is a great escalation beat. The children using Ann's own game against her creates satisfying ironic structure.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm going to break down this door.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What? No! Ron, we can just call the landlord!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I am the landlord now.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You're not the landlord!

jokes.text: Stand back, ladies! / Ron, no, no, no, no! That's dangerous! / Somebody in here's gotta have keys, right? / I have keys. Wha-- / Jerry.
jokes.setup: Ron is about to kick the door down; Ann stops him; Jerry inexplicably appears with keys
jokes.punchline: Jerry happens to have keys to the building — a completely coincidental saving grace — and Ron's pained 'Jerry.' acknowledges both gratitude and humiliation at needing Jerry
jokes.explanation: Ron's pained delivery of 'Jerry.' — the single name used as complete sentence — conveys everything: gratitude he can't express and resentment that he needs Jerry. Classic Parks running gag of everyone being dismissive of Jerry even when he helps.

dialogue.speaker: Kid
dialogue.line: The doll has a severe case of bad hair day syndrome. It's terminal. The only cure is a haircut.

jokes.text: I never thought I would say this, but I am so glad you're here. / Well, it's gotta be one of these, right?
jokes.setup: Ann sincerely compliments Jerry's presence for the first time
jokes.punchline: Jerry's response — 'it's gotta be one of these, right?' — while fumbling through his keys is oblivious to the rare praise, completely focused on the task. The joke is that Jerry doesn't even register the compliment.
jokes.explanation: Good Jerry character beat — when he finally gets a compliment, he's too anxious/focused to hear it. Consistent with the Parks running joke about Jerry being perpetually overlooked, now extended to him overlooking his own validation.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Easy, breezy, beautiful... CoverGirl.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, why did I just say that?

jokes.text: Ah, easy, breezy, beautiful. / That's the Covergirl slogan. I didn't mean to say that.
jokes.setup: Leslie reacts to the easy first part of loading a large refrigerator
jokes.punchline: She inadvertently quotes a cosmetics ad slogan, then immediately disavows it — the corporate catchphrase slipped out from deep in her consciousness
jokes.explanation: Good self-awareness joke — Leslie catching herself quoting a cosmetics slogan on a feminist mission, then immediately backpedaling. The specificity of Covergirl (vs. a generic slogan) makes it funnier. Leslie's embarrassment is earned.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, no, I got this. I'm like Rosa Parks, but for fridges.

jokes.text: You need a hand? / No, no, we don't need a hand. / What, you think Joan of Arc needed a hand? / Doing what?
jokes.setup: Dewey offers to help Leslie and April with the heavy fridge; Leslie refuses on feminist grounds
jokes.punchline: Leslie invokes Joan of Arc; April asks 'Doing what?' — a perfect deflation of Leslie's grandiloquence, pointing out that Joan of Arc's specific deeds don't map onto fridge-moving
jokes.explanation: 'Doing what?' is a precision-guided comedic missile — two words that expose the absurdity of Leslie's historical analogy without needing elaboration. April as the deflator of Leslie's rhetoric is a well-established dynamic used perfectly here.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, if I just... tip it back on the dolly wheels... and kind of shimmy it sideways...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: See? Stealth. Like a ninja. A very loud, grunting ninja.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Why is this so heavy? Did they fill it with sadness?

jokes.text: We are not leaving until this symbolic feminist obstacle is loaded onto that truck of women's advancement, and you can put that on the record, Shauna.
jokes.setup: Leslie cannot move the refrigerator but refuses to give up
jokes.punchline: Leslie reframes an immovable refrigerator as 'a symbolic feminist obstacle' and the garbage truck as 'a truck of women's advancement' — grandiose framing for a mundane physical problem
jokes.explanation: Peak Leslie — her ability to wrap any problem in the language of feminist struggle is maximally expressed here. 'Truck of women's advancement' is a very quotable phrase. The character integration score is very high because this joke works ONLY as Leslie; no other character would think or speak this way.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Ann, you are the most competent, dedicated, and... and beautiful woman I've ever met.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Ron, did you just call me beautiful?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: No. I said you were a... beautiful disaster. Of paperwork.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's not what you said.

jokes.text: Hey, Shauna, maybe not put this part on the record. You know, leave the earlier part on the record, but if we can't get this fridge onto the truck then maybe not put that on the record, and then just destroy the record altogether.
jokes.setup: After telling Shauna to put her feminist speech on the record, Leslie immediately starts walking it back
jokes.punchline: Leslie's escalating requests — from 'not this part' to 'destroy the record altogether' — reveal her publicity instincts overriding her feminist conviction in real-time
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback to the previous moment — Leslie said 'put that on the record' 30 seconds ago and is now desperately trying to un-record everything. The escalation to 'destroy the record altogether' is proportionate to her panic. Very character-specific anxiety about public image.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Ron, I heard what you said. You love me!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I said no such thing, Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You just called me Leslie!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Did I? Well, that changes nothing.

jokes.text: I'm gonna go ahead and decide what's on and off the record on my own. Cool?
jokes.setup: Leslie has been telling Shauna what to print and not print
jokes.punchline: Shauna calmly asserts basic journalistic independence with the casual 'Cool?' — the understatement of reclaiming editorial control is the joke
jokes.explanation: Shauna's flat assertion of independence capped with 'Cool?' is a good deadpan line. The casualness in the face of Leslie's frantic media management is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I have a deeply rooted fear of commitment.

dialogue.speaker: Kids
dialogue.line: Ron's scared! Ron's scared! Ron's scared of commitment!

jokes.text: I don't know why I thought sneaking up on it would work.
jokes.setup: Leslie has apparently tried to sneak up on the refrigerator to move it
jokes.punchline: Leslie reflects that this approach was, in retrospect, irrational — but the self-awareness doesn't explain why she tried it in the first place
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The visual of Leslie sneaking up on a refrigerator is wholly implied but completely vivid. The deadpan self-reflection ('I don't know why I thought...') is funnier than if we'd seen it. The comedy comes from Leslie having clearly done something insane and applying calm retrospective analysis. Very high quotability, excellent economy, and deeply character-specific — Leslie's relationship with her own bad ideas is perfectly captured.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I love breakfast food.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That doesn't mean I don't love meat.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I love 'em both equally.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Don't tell anyone.

jokes.text: This is the one. This is-- Oh! / Why do you have so many keys?
jokes.setup: Jerry is trying to unlock the door with what appears to be a massive keyring
jokes.punchline: Jerry keeps choosing the wrong key while the crisis continues; Ron questions why Jerry has so many keys
jokes.explanation: Functional Jerry-fumbling joke but not particularly original — the 'Jerry fails at simple task' beat is well-worn in the series. 'Why do you have so many keys?' is a decent line but the joke doesn't have a strong punchline. Competent but weak in the episode context.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't love her!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I mean, I respect her work ethic, her intelligence, her unwavering dedication to public service...

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: But that's not love. That's just... admiration. Professional admiration.

jokes.text: This is the one. This is-- Oh! / Why do you have so many keys? / [Jerry struggles with keys while children cause chaos]
jokes.setup: Ron and Ann need Jerry to open a locked door during the children's surgery emergency
jokes.punchline: Jerry has so many keys he can't find the right one under pressure — a competence failure joke that is both funny and characteristic of Jerry's uselessness in crises
jokes.explanation: A standard Jerry uselessness beat. Works within the show's running characterization of Jerry. Not particularly inventive but serviceable.

dialogue.speaker: Shauna
dialogue.line: I'm thinking we could have a really romantic dinner, just the two of us.

dialogue.speaker: Shauna
dialogue.line: Well, my ex will be there, and probably like fifteen of my closest friends, and maybe some people from my CrossFit gym...

jokes.text: You need to fix this. / It's not that bad. Nobody got hurt. / It's extremely bad! / I love this woman, and I just wanna show her that I'm capable of watching her children without something horrible happening.
jokes.setup: Ann confronts Ron about what just happened with the children
jokes.punchline: Ron accidentally reveals he loves Diane — the emotional admission slips out mid-argument in a way that is both a genuine character moment and a comedic revelation
jokes.explanation: The accidental love confession from Ron Swanson — a man who famously suppresses emotion — is a perfect misdirection. The argument about childcare produces an emotional revelation Ron didn't intend. Very character-specific: Ron of all people, accidentally, in an argument. The structure works because the confession is embedded in practical reasoning, not romantic declaration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We can't move the fridge. It's too heavy. So I guess we'll just have to eat all the food in it.

jokes.text: Did you just say you love Diane? / No. I did not. / Yes, you did! That is so cute! / For God's sake, Hanson, will you please focus on the larger problem?
jokes.setup: Ann catches Ron's accidental confession
jokes.punchline: Ron's flat denial ('No. I did not.') followed by Ann's genuine delight, followed by Ron calling her 'Hanson' (wrong name) in exasperated deflection — the wrong name is the comedic button
jokes.explanation: Ron calling Ann 'Hanson' in the heat of embarrassed deflection is a perfect callback to his earlier name confusion. His denial is so flat it's funny. 'For God's sake, Hanson' channels his exasperation while inadvertently being funny. The callback makes it richer on rewatch.

dialogue.speaker: Orin
dialogue.line: You see, what happened is you're all ghosts. You died in this house and now you're trapped here forever.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, what? That's not... we're not ghosts.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We're ghosts.

dialogue.speaker: Orin
dialogue.line: Yes, you're like small birds trapped in a house. Except you're dead.

jokes.text: Ron loves Mommy! / Girls, girls, I don't know what you think you heard, but please don't tell your mother what you incorrectly think you heard. / Ron loves-- Mommy! Ron loves Mommy! / I love nothing!
jokes.setup: The girls have heard Ron's accidental confession and immediately weaponize it
jokes.punchline: 'I love nothing!' — Ron's desperate, existential denial of all love is the perfect punchline, the most Ron Swanson sentence possible
jokes.explanation: The episode's funniest joke. 'I love nothing!' is perfectly Ron Swanson — a man whose identity is built on stoic self-sufficiency, forced by two children into the most ridiculous defensive position possible. The escalation from accidental confession → denial → children chanting → 'I love nothing!' is structurally flawless. The line is deeply character-specific (only Ron says this), perfectly economical, and highly quotable. This is the episode's standout moment and approaches the anchor example in quality.

dialogue.speaker: Bakery owner
dialogue.line: A bear is much bigger than a canary.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes, we all know that! Can we please just get back to the cupcakes?

jokes.text: I'm gonna have to start writing this up soon. Kinda sucks. I thought maybe we'd be done in time to grab a drink. / Oh! Have you been to Bistro d'Amour? It's really romantic. / Ooh. / Yeah, it was just gonna be you and me, my sister, a few people from work, and my ex-boyfriend. / That's really confusing.
jokes.setup: Chris suggests getting a drink; Shauna enthusiastically suggests a romantic spot
jokes.punchline: The 'romantic' venue suggestion is immediately loaded with her sister, coworkers, and ex-boyfriend — making it a group hang again, exactly the confusing modern dating behavior Chris was already struggling with
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the group hang confusion from the cold open. Shauna is doing it again — turning a romantic moment into a crowd event — and Chris's defeated 'That's really confusing' is a perfectly understated reaction. The ex-boyfriend detail is the escalating punchline detail.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Have you tried putting illegal drugs in it?

jokes.text: I guess I'll have to wait for tomorrow's paper to find out our status. / Why did I have to fall for somebody from the old media?
jokes.setup: Shauna says she'll decide what goes in the paper about their relationship
jokes.punchline: Chris laments falling for 'somebody from the old media' — treating Shauna's journalistic authority over their relationship as an inconvenience specific to her profession
jokes.explanation: 'Old media' as the problem — rather than the obvious issue of dating a reporter who covers you — is a funny tech-culture displacement. Chris treats print journalism as the specific obstacle, not journalistic ethics. Good character specificity and contemporary resonance.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hey Ben, can I borrow some money? No questions asked.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Uh, sure. What's it for?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Fireworks.

jokes.text: Maybe we should just eat the refrigerator. We start chewing now, we can finish before the sun comes up.
jokes.setup: Leslie and April are stuck unable to move the refrigerator
jokes.punchline: April proposes literally eating the refrigerator as a solution, with a casual timeline estimate
jokes.explanation: April's solution is perfectly absurdist — not just suggesting eating it, but adding a timeline ('before the sun comes up') that implies she's actually calculated this. The deadpan practicality of the timeline is what elevates it from simple absurdism. Very April.

dialogue.speaker: Diane
dialogue.line: Well, Ron, last week one of them set the kitchen on fire trying to make toast. So compared to that, this is fine.

jokes.text: You are two little canaries. / Those garbagemen couldn't even lift it. They are like giant bears. / Hold on. What do you mean? / Bears are bigger than canaries, yes? So if bears can't lift the-- / No, I understand animal sizes.
jokes.setup: An older man dismisses Leslie and April as 'canaries' compared to 'bears' (the garbagemen)
jokes.punchline: Leslie interrupts his animal-size logic to clarify she understands comparative animal sizes — the joke is that the man thinks she's failing to follow the metaphor when she's actually just processing the relevant information
jokes.explanation: 'No, I understand animal sizes' is a great Leslie line — cutting through the man's condescending metaphor to focus on the actual new information. The man's earnest explanation ('Bears are bigger than canaries, yes?') makes him a great foil. The joke is in Leslie's precise, efficient dismissal of the irrelevant part of the metaphor.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, April, a gift! How thoughtful!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: It's garbage.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, what?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Literally garbage. I found it in the dumpster behind the Sweetums building.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh.

jokes.text: Those Sanitation goons set us up.
jokes.setup: Leslie realizes the garbagemen intentionally assigned them an unmovable fridge
jokes.punchline: 'Sanitation goons' — Leslie's sudden adoption of tough-guy language for municipal garbage workers is an incongruous register that's funny in its indignation
jokes.explanation: 'Sanitation goons' is a mild but effective character-voice joke — Leslie rarely uses gangster register, so the word 'goons' from her is incongruous enough to land. Efficient but not deeply crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Welcome to Tom's Bistro. We have the finest cuisine in Pawnee. Our chef trained in Paris for twelve years. We also have a full bar with craft cocktails made by mixologists who actually know what they're doing. And if you're not satisfied with your meal, we will personally fly to your house and cook you another one. Tom's Bistro: nothing but net.

jokes.text: Look, all we have to do is get some PCP. You can move anything on angel dust. My cousin Hesen, he beat off five cops on that stuff.
jokes.setup: Leslie and April brainstorm solutions for moving the refrigerator
jokes.punchline: April suggests PCP as a practical solution, backs it up with a specific family anecdote involving five police officers, and treats it as completely reasonable logistics
jokes.explanation: Classic April dark humor — PCP as a logistics solution is unexpected, but the specific detail of 'cousin Hesen' and 'five cops' makes it vivid and funnier. The anecdote is delivered as a product testimonial. Very character-specific (April has this kind of family) and highly quotable.

jokes.text: Guys, I think I just dribbled up an idea. / No, double dribbled it. / Yeah, you have learned nothing about basketball.
jokes.setup: Tom has a realization and uses a basketball metaphor
jokes.punchline: Andy and Ben immediately correct his metaphor — 'double dribbled it' — and then editorialize on his broader basketball ignorance
jokes.explanation: The pun on 'dribbled up an idea' is mild but functional, and the basketball-specific correction (double dribbled) is character-consistent for a geek and a jock to make. 'You have learned nothing about basketball' is a funny final verdict.

jokes.text: You're a good friend, Ben. / Oh, thanks. / Can I borrow $1,500? / You're not allowed to ask what it's for. / Fireworks.
jokes.setup: Tom compliments Ben, then immediately leverages the compliment for a large loan
jokes.punchline: Tom instructs Ben not to ask what it's for — implying something suspicious — then immediately volunteers 'Fireworks' anyway, which somehow doesn't help
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke structure. The compliment-to-loan pivot is already funny; 'You're not allowed to ask what it's for' raises the comedic stakes by implying something worse than fireworks; then 'Fireworks' arrives as a punchline that somehow doesn't reassure. The structure has three distinct beat: setup (compliment), misdirection (you're not allowed to ask), punchline (fireworks). Highly quotable, perfectly Tom, excellent economy. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in structure and quotability.

jokes.text: First of all, everyone is fine. / No one got hurt, but there was an incident. / Oh, my God. What happened?
jokes.setup: Ann has to explain to Diane what happened with the children
jokes.punchline: The pre-emptive 'First of all, everyone is fine / No one got hurt, but there was an incident' is a comic formula that implies something terrible happened, making Diane's 'Oh, my God' the expected reaction and the actual incident funnier in contrast
jokes.explanation: The 'First of all, everyone is fine' formula is a well-worn comedy trope — it's functional misdirection but not particularly original. Works as scene setup rather than a strong joke on its own. The comedy here is largely in what follows.

jokes.text: Well, who has been having fun with scissors? / Us! / Ann taught us how to be doctors! / Yay!
jokes.setup: Diane walks into the room to find the aftermath
jokes.punchline: The children enthusiastically implicate Ann — 'Ann taught us how to be doctors!' — with 'Yay!' as an exclamation, framing what was clearly chaos as a celebration
jokes.explanation: The children's cheerful implication of Ann is a good callback to her earlier confident parenting advice. Their enthusiasm makes the situation worse in the funniest way — they're proud of their surgery. 'Yay!' as a celebration of chaos is well-placed.

jokes.text: You're not mad? / No, it's fine. They're kids. Once, Zoe put Ivy in the dryer, so...
jokes.setup: Ann braces for Diane's anger at the scissor incident
jokes.punchline: Diane's 'Once, Zoe put Ivy in the dryer, so...' — a casually mentioned child-endangerment incident delivered as 'kids will be kids' — implies her baseline is far more dangerous than scissors
jokes.explanation: The dryer confession is a perfectly calibrated dark joke — delivered with complete casualness by Diane, implying the scissors are nothing compared to her daughters' normal behavior. 'So...' trailing off instead of completing the thought is the ideal economy choice. The specificity (Zoe put IVY in the dryer, not just 'a sibling') makes it vivid and funnier.

jokes.text: This is why I love you. / Oh. / Well, I love you, too.
jokes.setup: Diane reacts warmly to Ron's obvious love for her children's wellbeing
jokes.punchline: Diane says 'I love you' casually, totally naturally. Ron's 'Oh.' suggests his brain has seized. Then his 'Well, I love you, too' — delivered presumably with stunned formality — is the comedic button, paying off the entire Ron-loves-Diane arc of the episode
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the episode's emotional/comedic arc. After Ron denied loving anything ('I love nothing!'), Diane casually says 'I love you' and Ron just... reciprocates. The comedy is in the total reversal — the man who declared 'I love nothing' 10 minutes ago now saying 'Well, I love you, too' with formal inevitability. The 'Oh.' beat implies the emotional processing happening in real time. This is character comedy at its best — the joke IS the character growth. Rewatch bonus is very high for the context.

jokes.text: That's my cue.
jokes.setup: Ron and Diane exchange 'I love you's' in front of Ann
jokes.punchline: Ann's deadpan 'That's my cue' and immediate exit is the perfect third-wheel acknowledgment — she recognizes the romantic moment and evacuates with zero drama
jokes.explanation: A small, efficient button on the emotional scene. Three words, perfectly placed. Ann's awareness and graceful exit is good comic timing even if the joke itself is simple. Maximum economy.

jokes.text: City manager Chris Traeger was present for this event, and has a personal relationship with the author. / Okay, that's pretty good, right? 'Personal relationship.' / It's not romantic. / But it is descriptive. No, it's not even descriptive.
jokes.setup: Chris reads Shauna's disclaimer about their relationship
jokes.punchline: Chris's back-and-forth self-reassessment — 'it is descriptive... No, it's not even descriptive' — shows him spiraling over the vagueness of 'personal relationship' in real-time
jokes.explanation: Good Chris anxiety joke — his immediate reversal on whether 'personal relationship' is descriptive is a nice character beat. Consistent with the episode's running theme of Chris not being able to handle ambiguous relationship status.

jokes.text: I know you're not used to this, but maybe you should just try to keep it chill and see what happens. / Great advice. / Impossible to follow, but great advice.
jokes.setup: Leslie advises Chris on his relationship anxiety
jokes.punchline: Chris immediately affirms the advice ('Great advice.') then immediately admits it's completely inapplicable to him ('Impossible to follow') — the two-beat reversal perfectly captures his self-aware inability to be chill
jokes.explanation: Excellent Chris character joke. The two-beat structure — validate, then immediately self-negate — is very clean. 'Impossible to follow, but great advice' is a highly quotable, character-specific admission of his anxiety. The joke lands harder because Chris is the one saying it about himself.

jokes.text: So do you think the soup kitchen could use that fridge? / I mean, April and I were gonna haul it onto the truck effortlessly, but if you need it... / Absolutely. This is a godsend. / Grab a side, ladies. / I think all of us can get it on the truck.
jokes.setup: Leslie has to admit she can't move the fridge; she spins it as a gift
jokes.punchline: 'April and I were gonna haul it onto the truck effortlessly, but if you need it...' — Leslie saves face by framing her failure as generosity, with the mock-modest 'effortlessly' being the comedic lie
jokes.explanation: Leslie's face-saving spin is a great character joke — she turns the fridge she could not move into a charitable gift, complete with fictional 'effortless' hauling. 'But if you need it...' is the perfect faux-generous phrasing.

jokes.text: And it's trash. / It's filled with trash. / Maybe there's something on the bottom here. Let me see-- No, just trash.
jokes.setup: April gives Leslie a 'present' to commemorate their feminist victory
jokes.punchline: The present is literally garbage — trash from the route — and Leslie investigates for a hidden meaningful item before confirming it's just trash all the way down
jokes.explanation: A perfect April-gives-Leslie-a-gift joke. April's idea of a commemorative present is literal trash from their day of garbage work. The comedic extension — Leslie hoping there's something meaningful at the bottom, then confirming 'No, just trash' — is a great structure. Very character-specific for April (this is exactly what April would do) and for Leslie (she'd look anyway).

jokes.text: And it's trash. It's filled with trash. Maybe there's something on the bottom here. Let me see-- No, just trash.
jokes.setup: April gives Leslie a present to commemorate their feminist victory on the garbage route
jokes.punchline: The 'present' is simply trash — April has given Leslie garbage as a gift, and Leslie's methodical search for something meaningful at the bottom ('Let me see--') finds only more trash
jokes.explanation: A wonderful April/Leslie joke. April's gift of literal garbage is perfect April — nihilistic, trollish, but delivered with apparent sincerity. Leslie's patient excavation of the trash looking for meaning ('Maybe there's something on the bottom here. Let me see-- No, just trash.') is the ideal Leslie response. Their dynamic in 6 words: 'No, just trash.' Strong character integration for both.

jokes.text: Tom's post-game press conference product placement speech: 'Dope suits, pocket squares, gingham shirts, glasses with no lenses, tiny cardigans, fedoras... Look at this watch! Whatever swag you need, you can rent at Rent-A-Swag. Now, that's basketball.'
jokes.setup: Tom has managed to insert himself into a kids' basketball post-game news segment
jokes.punchline: Tom's Rent-A-Swag infomercial hijacks a children's sports segment with a list of very specific fashion items, capped by 'Now, that's basketball' — a completely non-sequitur sign-off that has nothing to do with basketball
jokes.explanation: 'Glasses with no lenses' and 'tiny cardigans' are great specific details in Tom's swag inventory. 'Now, that's basketball' as a fashion-to-basketball non-sequitur sign-off is the perfectly absurd button — it's the standard sports broadcast sign-off applied to a fashion ad. Tom using a kids' sports broadcast to advertise his rental store is entirely on-brand. High character integration score.

jokes.text: Tom Haverford hijacks a child's post-game interview to advertise Rent-A-Swag at a kids' basketball game: 'We've got everything: Dope suits, pocket squares, Gingham shirts, glasses with no lenses, Tiny cardigans, Fedoras... Look at this watch!'
jokes.setup: A child reporter is conducting a post-game interview with the star player
jokes.punchline: Tom hijacks the child's sports interview to deliver a full Rent-A-Swag advertisement, complete with an itemized product listing and the declaration 'Now, that's basketball' — having no basketball connection
jokes.explanation: A great Tom Haverford ending. His complete willingness to exploit a children's sports broadcast for brand advertising — at full infomercial pace — is perfect. 'Glasses with no lenses' and 'Tiny cardigans' as earnest product offerings, capped with 'Now, that's basketball' (which has nothing to do with anything he said), is excellent character comedy. High character integration.

tmdb_overview: Leslie and April handle a garbage route, while Tom asks Andy and Ben to teach him about basketball. Meanwhile, Ron is left to watch Diane's kids while their babysitter is out of town.
insight: Women in garbage lands 84 through character-driven comedy, 70 jokes in 25 minutes.
